Hmm this doesn't sound right. Everything in "wait for all" works behind microtasks.
Wait for all calls [PreformPromiseThen](https://tc39.es/ecma262/multipage/control-abstraction-objects.html#sec-performpromisethen) which calls [HostEnqueuePromiseJob](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/webappapis.html#hostenqueuepromisejob) which queues a microtask.

I missed that -- you're right, it does not run sync. But it still runs in the same microtask, no? So the `PerformPromiseThen` should execute in [step 12](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#commit-a-navigate-event:~:text=Clean%20up%20after%20running%20script%20given%20navigation%27s%20relevant%20settings%20object%2E,-Per) of #commit-a-navigate-event, which is before `location.href` returns.

> I missed that -- you're right, it does not run sync. But it still runs in the same microtask, no? So the `PerformPromiseThen` should execute in [step 12](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#commit-a-navigate-event:~:text=Clean%20up%20after%20running%20script%20given%20navigation%27s%20relevant%20settings%20object%2E,-Per) of #commit-a-navigate-event, which is before `location.href` returns.

No, not the same microtask... `PerformPromiseThen` queues a new microtask to run the success/failure steps. The tests are correct IMO

WaitForAll queues one microtask in this case. https://webidl.spec.whatwg.org/#wait-for-all step 9.4
That is now in the queue, and that microtask will handle failureStep and fire navigateerror.
Now, execution in the test continues, and Promise.resolve().then(() => recorder.record("promise microtask")); runs. That is another microtask in the queue. Now, await happens and both microtasks run and navigateerror is fired before "promise microtask"

OK gotcha. So changing to https://webidl.spec.whatwg.org/#waiting-for-all-promise would fix this because it would require another `then` on the returned promise which would flip the order. Did I get it right?
I think the spec is fine. That gives the least surprising behavior to web developers.  Chromium needs to change to follow the spec.

That's fine with me. @natechapin?

I think that's ok. However, I don't think chromium is currently set up to differentiate between [wait for all](https://webidl.spec.whatwg.org/#wait-for-all) and [get a promise for waiting for all](https://webidl.spec.whatwg.org/#waiting-for-all-promise). This might be a slightly more involved change.

A few things about this:
- There is a [note](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#navigate-event-firing:wait-for-all-3) in the spec precisely about this.
- The only other place which uses "wait for all" is WebBluetooth (the navigation API handlers/precommitHandlers is the only place in the HTML spec that does this)
- There are a few other callers that reference "get a promise waiting for all"

Given the above, I think changing the spec would actually be better for everyone. Perhaps we can retire "wait for all" at some point and only have "get a promise waiting for all".

I'd argue that using #wait-for-all produces the most consistent timing behavior, as @smaug---- notes. The fact that something that immediately rejects gets scheduled after something that hasn't even been scheduled yet is very surprising.

Counter argument: this is not consistent with how developers can create this flow themselves.

```js
// This resolves to "after"
Promise.race([
  Promise.all([Promise.resolve("success")]),
  Promise.resolve("after")
])

// This resolves to "success"
Promise.race([
  Promise.resolve("success"),
  Promise.resolve("after")
])
```

Isn't it a bit weird that the platform emulates the second behavior in some cases?

It's neither weird nor an emulation.

The major difference is that we're not working with promises, we're working with callbacks, which we can expect to not be bound by how `Promise.all` works.  A callback based comparison with how this algorithm works would instead be more similar to:
```javascript
const order = [];
// order becomes ["callback", "promise"]
Promise.all([
  Promise.all([Promise.reject().finally(() => order.push("callback")), 
               new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 1000)).finally(() => order.push("timeout"))]),
  Promise.resolve().finally(() => order.push("promise"))
])

const order = [];
// order becomes ["callback", "promise", "timeout"]
Promise.all([
  Promise.all([Promise.resolve().finally(() => order.push("callback")), 
               new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, 1000)).finally(() => order.push("timeout"))]),
  Promise.resolve().finally(() => order.push("promise"))
])
```
I'm intentionally focusing on the rejection case, because in the `Promise.all` example above:
```javascript
Promise.race([
  Promise.all([Promise.reject("reject")]),
  Promise.resolve("after")
])
```
would resolve to `after`, not capturing rejection at all. This makes this example not at all behave as the navigation callbacks do, since we'll never not report a failure.

If a developer would want to re-create this flow, they would basically just implement `Promise.waitForAll`. In particular, using `#wait-for-all` allows us to capture a potential error case sooner which enables users to have more control over the flow of navigations.
OK this is fine with me but I want to check in with @natechapin re. implementability in chrome given that this is the first case in the web platform where the difference is web observable.

That's very interesting. We ran into a similar issue when implementing #inner-navigate-event-firing-algorithm, where we needed to [delay the call to #wait-for-all](https://searchfox.org/firefox-main/rev/0516e0135dab129510c0dee588ea75ffa62f24c8/dom/navigation/Navigation.cpp#1386) in case there was an ongoing method tracker. We thought this was a quirk with Gecko, and tried to follow the intent of the spec. If Blink also suffers from this I start learning towards something being underspecced. This is another spec issue, not related to this one. 

If there is a requirement that onsuccess should fire after reactions to the committed promise this should be made explicit in spec. I think onerror doesn't have this requirement, so possibly Gecko's solution isn't entirely optional and only the success callback should be a reaction to the committed promise, if such exists. Implicitly betting that the extra lap on the microtask queue fixes this is not a solution, especially for fast failure handling and non-method tracker navigations. 

In the end these order issues are an inherent problem in the difference in nature between events and promises.

I'll file a new issue for this.

> I wonder if the thing we need to remove here is actually the dummy promise when the handler list is empty... that's the thing that adds the strange extra microtask and makes a synchronous navigation become async. Promise.all([]) should be exactly one microtask, unlike Promise.all([Promise.resolve()]).

This doesn't change anything, Blink still has the same bug, where the /synchronous/ navigation claims `onnavigateerror` but the "navigation" (in this case intercepted) still goes through. So really our entire discussion in this issue is just a realization that this issue should just be closed as works for me, and we should fix the tests because the spec is fine.

The interesting part is when we change the synchronous navigation to a synchronous navigation that also creates a method tracker, namely `navigation.navigate('#1')`, because in this case Gecko also aborts the first navigation. This is out of necessity, because without it it isn't possible, as spec is written, to entirely run the success callback steps. This is in fact a spec bug, and is exactly issue [#11864](https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11864).

I'll keep this issue open until the test change requests have gone through, and I'll make sure to link those when I have a PR for them.

`navigateerror` doesn't mean "the navigation didn't go through".
E.g. with intercept handler rejections, the navigation "goes through" (as in, committed), and the entries are there in the history, but the navigation has "errored" because some of the handlers failed.

Conceptually, when you perform multiple navigations synchronously one after the other, it's arguable whether the first navigation was "successful". It has definitely been "committed", but the author had no opportunity to respond to it (e.g. react to its `committed` promise) so it's not entirely successful.

I wouldn't rush to change the tests to match the spec here before we resolve on this. It's the first observable occurrence of "wait for all" without a wrapping promise and I want to make sure we're not making a mistake that can break existing sites that use the navigation API.

... in other words, a successful navigation *is* asynchronous (as per https://github.com/whatwg/html/issues/11845#issuecomment-3480421420) and can be interrupted after commit, while *committing* a navigation can be synchronous in some cases.

I'd also like to hear @jakearchibald about this as someone who was involved in the original design of the navigation API
(I've inherited it from Domenic so might miss some of the original context).

> navigateerror doesn't mean "the navigation didn't go through".

[Yes it does](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/indices.html#event-navigateerror:~:text=Fired%20when%20a%20navigation%20does%20not%20complete%20successfully)

> Conceptually, when you perform multiple navigations synchronously one after the other, it's arguable whether the first navigation was "successful"

No it isn't, since the navigations can be observed, e.g through `onhashchange`.

Preamble: I think it is generally slightly weird when events are dispatched from a microtask, although there is precedent for that (e.g., `slotchange`). I also don't like it that navigations can be synchronous. Neither can be changed.

I agree with @farre that it is weird to dispatch a `navigateerror` event if the navigation in fact succeeded and results in a `hashchange` event.

I suspect WebKit can align on either timing, as long as the specification and tests are clear.

> I agree with [@farre](https://github.com/farre) that it is weird to dispatch a `navigateerror` event if the navigation in fact succeeded and results in a `hashchange` event.

That can also happen regardless of this issue, if the navigation is intercepted and aborted before all the handlers complete.
The navigation API extended the concept of "successful navigation" beyond being committed (which is what would trigger a `hashchange`).

It can be argued that a navigation that was preempted by another navigation before the author had a chance to respond to its committed/finished promises is "aborted" in a sense (after commit), as if it had empty handlers.

But at this point this is not a hill I would die on and I'm ready to change the blink implementation to what the spec says.
